chunks: Ahmad ibn Idris, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn Sayf, from Muhammad ibn Ubayd, who said:

I wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) asking him about the sighting (of God) and what is reported by the general (Sunni) Muslims and the specific ones (Shias), and I asked him to explain that to me.

So he wrote in his own handwriting: All have agreed, without dispute among them, that knowledge from the aspect of sighting is self-evident. So if it were permitted that God be seen with the eye, such knowledge would occur necessarily. Then that knowledge would not be free from either being iman (faith) or not being iman.

If that knowledge from the aspect of sighting were iman, then the knowledge in this world acquired through attainment would not be iman, because it is its opposite — so there would be no believer in this world, since they have not seen God, Mighty is His mention.

And if that knowledge from the aspect of sighting is not iman, then this knowledge acquired through attainment would not be free from diminishing in this world and not diminishing in the Hereafter. So this is evidence that God, Mighty and Majestic, cannot be seen with the eye, since the eye leads to what we have described.

key_terms.إِيمَان: Iman — faith, belief; the state of being a mu'min (believer)
key_terms.الرُّؤْيَة: Ru'yah — the sighting/vision of God; the theological debate about whether God can be seen physically, especially in the afterlife
key_terms.الِاكْتِسَاب: Al-iktisab — acquisition, the process of attaining knowledge through study, reason, and transmitted learning
key_terms.الْخَاصَّة: Al-khassa — 'the specific/particular ones', a technical term referring to Shia Muslims
key_terms.الْعَامَّة: Al-'amma — 'the general/common ones', a technical term used by Shia scholars to refer to Sunni Muslims
key_terms.الْمَعَاد: Al-ma'ad — the Return; the Hereafter, the Day of Resurrection
key_terms.الْمَعْرِفَة: Ma'rifa — recognition, knowledge, gnosis; particularly the intuitive or direct knowledge that comes from experiencing something
key_terms.عَزَّ وَجَلَّ: Azza wa jalla — 'Mighty and Majestic', an honorific for God

ai.seo_question: Can God be seen with the eye according to Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam Ali al-Rida (peace be upon him), the eighth Imam, responded in writing to Muhammad ibn Ubayd's inquiry about whether God can be physically seen — a major point of contention between the Sunni and Shia traditions. The Imam employs a careful logical argument (a dilemma): if sight-based knowledge of God is a form of iman, then no one in this world would be a believer; if it is not iman, then it would be subject to the same limitations as other acquired knowledge. Either way, the conclusion is that God cannot be seen with the physical eye. This hadith, notable as a handwritten response from the Imam, reflects the Shia theological position of divine transcendence (tanzih) and the Imam's role as the definitive authority in settling theological controversies.
